The pakhawaj is a barrel-shaped, double-headed membranophone from the Indian subcontinent, one of the Indian two-headed drums; earlier forms were made of clay, with animal skin (often goatskin) around the sides. The player sits cross-legged on the floor and lays the drum across the body in front; right-handers usually put the larger bass head on the left and the treble head on the right, and the bass head may be smeared with fresh wheat dough to strengthen the bass. It is most used in dhrupad Indian classical music, and less often as rhythm accompaniment for music and dance such as kathak, odissi and Marathi.
帕卡瓦吉鼓源自南亞，與東南亞海洋地區的肯當鼓及印度其他雙面鼓同屬雙面鼓系統。其較: The pakhawaj comes from South Asia and belongs, with the kendang of maritime Southeast Asia and other Indian two-headed drums, to the two-headed drum system. Its earlier form was made of clay; the name comes from Prakrit, the corresponding Sanskrit word meaning 'an instrument with one side', and it has cognates in Telugu, Tamil and Kannada. In the fourteenth century some drum makers changed the body material from clay to wood, and the new name 'pakhavaj' appeared, while the old name 'mridang' stayed in use. The recitation syllables and the playing differ between schools, such as those of Nana Panse and Natdwara.

The heads are covered with animal skin, commonly goatskin; the bass head is smeared with fresh wheat dough to strengthen the bass. 帕卡瓦吉鼓為膜鳴雙面鼓，音色低沈、圓潤且泛音豐富。低音面塗新鮮小麥麵團，擊打時產: The pakhawaj is a double-headed membranophone with a low, round timbre rich in overtones. The bass head is smeared with fresh wheat dough and gives a lively bass when struck; the treble head, because the skin varies in thickness, can sound at least two notes a semitone apart, with different pitches at the centre and near the rim. In playing, the bass head is struck with the whole palm and the treble head with changing fingers or the whole hand to make different drum sounds; a damping stroke suppresses the resonance. Compared with the tabla the tuning method is similar, but the bass head is played with the whole palm rather than the fingertips and relies on the dough layer to strengthen the bass.

演奏者盤腿坐地，將鼓橫放身前；右撇子把較大低音面置左、高音面置右，必要時在高音面: The player sits cross-legged on the floor with the drum lying across the body in front; right-handers put the larger bass head on the left and the treble head on the right, and if need be rest a small cushion under the treble head. The bass head is smeared with fresh wheat dough to strengthen the bass; tuning adjusts the tensioning straps with wooden wedges, and the treble head can give notes a semitone apart depending on where it is struck. Beginners first memorise rhythm cycles as syllables and practise the basic patterns before moving on to fast phrases; the left hand strikes the bass head with the whole palm and the right hand uses different fingerings on the treble head, while traditionally the palm is also used to get a pure tone.
